name: Jay Gould

summary.text: Jay Gould (1836–1892) was an American railroad financier. In 1868, in alliance with Daniel Drew and James Fisk, he took part in the 'Erie War' against Cornelius Vanderbilt: the Erie directors issued convertible bonds that were converted into new stock and sold on the market, moved the company's cash and books to Jersey City to escape New York court orders, and secured a New York law legalising the stock issues, which Britannica says Gould obtained by bribing legislators. After a July 1868 settlement that compensated Vanderbilt, Gould and Fisk ended up in control of the Erie. Gould was later involved in the 1869 gold corner and controlled the Union Pacific and Western Union.

facts.claim: Britannica states that Gould's financial manipulations included the issue of fraudulent stock and the payment of lavish bribes to New York state legislators to legalise that stock's sale.
facts.quote: Gould engaged in outrageous financial manipulations, including the issue of fraudulent stock and the payment of lavish bribes to New York state legislators to legalize that stock's sale.

facts.claim: In 1868 Drew, in alliance with Gould and Fisk, manufactured 50,000 shares of Erie stock and dumped them on the market; Gould then obtained passage of a bill in Albany legalising what they had done.
facts.quote: Drew, in an alliance with Gould and Fisk, manufactured 50,000 shares of Erie stock and dumped them on the market. Gould was able to bribe legislators in Albany to secure passage of a bill legalizing what they had done.

facts.claim: Convertible bonds were the instrument used because bonds could be sold below par while stock could not, so the directors could dispose of them at any price; one account records an executive-committee vote to issue $10,000,000 in convertible bonds at 72½.
facts.quote: Because bonds could be sold below par while stock could not, convertible bonds could be disposed of by the directors at any price.

facts.claim: In February–March 1868 Judge George G. Barnard, at the request of Vanderbilt's representative Frank Work, enjoined the Erie from issuing new stock or converting bonds to stock, while a Brooklyn judge ordered the conversions to continue; on 10 March 1868 the Erie officers crossed to Jersey City with the bond proceeds, stock books and printing plates.
facts.quote: On March 10, the Erie officers took the ferry to New Jersey with the convertible-bond proceeds, the stock books, and the printing plates

facts.claim: A railroad chronology records that on 21 April 1868 New York Governor Reuben E. Fenton signed an act legalising the unauthorised Erie Railway stock issues.
facts.quote: New York Gov. Reuben E. Fenton signed an act legalizing the unauthorized Erie Railway stock issues

sources.title: A General Chronology of the Pennsylvania Railroad Company: 1868

facts.claim: Under the July 1868 settlement Vanderbilt was compensated from the Erie treasury for the stock he had bought; Gould and Fisk gained control of the railroad and Drew retired.
facts.quote: Gould and Fisk gained ultimate control of the railroad, pushing Drew to retire while paying back Vanderbilt for his watered down stocks.

sources.title: The Erie War (1868): Vanderbilt, Gould, Drew & Fisk

connections.claim: Gould, with Drew and Fisk, defeated Vanderbilt's 1868 attempt to buy control of the Erie by issuing new stock; the July 1868 settlement paid Vanderbilt out of the Erie treasury.
connections.quote: Vanderbilt was paid out of the Erie treasury and given two board seats

sources.title: The Erie War (1868): Vanderbilt, Gould, Drew & Fisk

connections.claim: Gould was allied with Erie treasurer Daniel Drew and James Fisk in the 1868 issue of 50,000 new Erie shares.
connections.quote: Drew, in an alliance with Gould and Fisk, manufactured 50,000 shares of Erie stock

connections.claim: Gould and James Fisk together ended up in control of the Erie after 1868 and then joined forces with William 'Boss' Tweed and Peter Sweeney.
connections.quote: Gould ended up in control of the railroad, and he and Fisk then joined forces with William ("Boss") Tweed and Peter Sweeney.

openQuestions: The site says $10 million in convertible bonds became 'roughly 100,000 new Erie shares'; Britannica says 50,000 shares, while a chronology lists two $5 million blocks (February and 9 March 1868). The total should be checked against Adams's 'Chapters of Erie'.

The site attributes to Gustavus Myers a satchel of $500,000 in greenbacks at Albany; the Myers chapter was returned by search but the satchel figure was not in the text returned. Verify in Myers directly.
Settlement price to Vanderbilt varies across sources ($120 per share, $70 per share, or $2.5 million cash plus securities for 50,000 shares).
The 'Erie Bill' date is given as 13 April (passage) and 21 April 1868 (signature).
The site's '$6–7 million of company cash' taken to Jersey City was not quantified in the sources consulted.
